You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

*   Goal: $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$, $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$, $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Best design so far: `SSHI_FullBridge_Zener` (topology `40eae91a637a`).
    *   Issues with `SSHI_FullBridge_Zener`:
        *   S3 ripple: $0.06152\text{V}$ (limit $0.05\text{V}$).
        *   S5 settled: $0.02237\text{V}$ (limit $0.02\text{V}$).
    *   The current topology is an SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) based on a full-bridge. SSHI typically increases the voltage extracted from the piezo.
    *   The failing constraints (ripple and settled) are very close to the limits.

    *   S3: Strong excitation (Ip = 100 uA), light load (RL = 2200 kOhm).
    *   S5: Low frequency (f = 80 Hz), nominal load (RL = 470 kOhm).
    *   In S3, the light load means the storage capacitor $C_{out}$ takes longer to discharge, but the high input power creates higher voltage spikes or ripple.
    *   In S5, the low frequency might cause the mean output to drift or fluctuate more over the two windows (0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge_Zener` has:
        *   Full bridge (D1-D4)
        *   L1 and S1 for SSHI inversion (pzp -> n1 -> pzn).
        *   Zener clamp DZ1 (0 to out).
        *   C1 (out to 0).
    *   Actually, looking at the components:
        *   `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn`. This is a standard full-bridge rectifier.
        *   `L1: pzp -> n1`, `S1: n1 -> pzn`. This is an inverter branch in parallel with the piezo.
    *   The SSHI inversion helps flip the voltage across the piezo capacitor $C_p$ to extract more energy.

    *   To reduce ripple ($v_{pp}$), we usually increase $C_{out}$ or improve the voltage regulation.
    *   To improve the "settled" metric ($dv$), we need the system to reach a steady state faster or have less drift.
    *   Wait, the Zener clamp is at 3.3V. The current $C_{out}$ is $9.33 \mu\text{F}$ (wait, it says $9.33\text{e-07}$ which is $0.933 \mu\text{F}$).

    *   *Idea 1: Improve Ripple/Stability by adding a low-pass filter or increasing capacitance (though the optimizer handles values).*
    *   *Idea 2: Try a different SSHI configuration.*
    *   The current SSHI configuration is: Inverter in parallel with the piezo, feeding into a full bridge.
    *   Let's look at the "Standard" SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor). Usually, the inductor is used to flip the voltage across the piezo *before* rectification.
    *   Looking at the components again:
        *   $C_p$ is between pzp and pzn.
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ are in parallel with $C_p$ (from pzp to pzn via n1).
        *   The rectifier is connected to pzp and pzn.
        *   This is a valid SSHI implementation.

    *   The failures are marginal.
    *   S3 Ripple: $0.061\text{V}$ vs $0.05\text{V}$.
    *   S5 Settled: $0.022\text{V}$ vs $0.02\text{V}$.

    *   Maybe change the rectification to a half-bridge if the power allows, to reduce losses? But we already passed $v_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$.
    *   Maybe a better way to clamp the voltage? The Zener is at 3.3V. If $v_{out}$ is near 3.3V, the ripple might be affected. In S3, $v_{avg} = 3.38\text{V}$, $v_{max} = 3.41\text{V}$. The Zener is active. When the Zener clamps, it can introduce non-linearities that might affect the settled value or ripple.
    *   However, the requirement is $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. The Zener DZ33 is at 3.3V.
    *   If we increase the Zener voltage? No, DZ33 is the only model provided.

    *   The current SSHI setup uses a full bridge. A "Parallel-SSHI" (PSSHI) or a "Series-SSHI" (SSHI) usually uses a switch and a diode.
    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" if the current one is too "aggressive" in S3.
    *   Alternatively, let's try a different inversion circuit. The current one is $L$ in series with $S$.

    *   When the Zener conducts, $v_{out}$ is clamped. The ripple $v_{pp}$ in S3 is $61\text{mV}$.
    *   Maybe a larger storage capacitor would help, but the optimizer should have found that.
    *   Wait, if the Zener is clamping, the ripple is determined by the Zener's dynamic resistance and the source.

    *   Could we use a different topology to get $v_{out}$ slightly lower than 3.3V in S3?
    *   The current design has $v_{avg} = 3.38\text{V}$ in S3.
    *   If we use a different rectifier or a different switching strategy?
    *   Actually, if we reduce the efficiency of the SSHI slightly, $v_{out}$ might drop below the Zener threshold, potentially reducing the ripple caused by the Zener clamping.
    *   But the optimizer already tried to tune $t_{on}$ and $\text{phase}$.

    *   Let's try a "Buck-Boost" style or a "Charge Pump" style? No, that's too complex.
    *   What about a "Synchronous Rectifier" (using switches instead of diodes) to reduce the voltage drop and then use the Zener? (Wait, we only have 2 SYNC controllers).
    *   The current design uses 1 SYNC for the inversion and 4 diodes for the rectifier.
    *   What if we use a Synchronous Rectifier?
        *   Switch 1: pzp to out
        *   Switch 2: pzn to out
        *   Switch 3: pzp to 0
        *   Switch 4: pzn to 0
        *   (Requires 4 switches, which is the limit).
        *   But we need a SYNC to control them. We only have 2 SYNCs.
        *   We could use SYNC1 for "pos" (close S1 and S4) and SYNC2 for "neg" (close S2 and S3).
        *   This would replace the full bridge.
        *   However, the SSHI inverter also needs a SYNC. That would be 3 SYNCs. (Limit is 2).

    *   The current SSHI is: $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with $C_p$.
    *   What if we use a "Half-Bridge" rectifier? (2 diodes).
    *   If the piezo is floating (pzn not grounded), we need a full bridge.
    *   If we ground pzn, we can use a half bridge. But the piezo is a current source between pzp and pzn. If we ground pzn, we only get half the energy? No, the current still flows. But the voltage $V_{pzn}$ would be 0.
    *   Wait, the reference design FBR is a full bridge.

    *   Let's look at the "settled" failure in S5. $dv = 0.022\text{V}$.
    *   S5 is low frequency (80 Hz).
    *   A lower frequency means the charging pulses are further apart.
    *   Maybe adding a second capacitor or a different configuration?

    *   What if we use a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson charge pump)?
    *   Piezo -> D1 -> C_fly -> D2 -> out.
    *   This is usually for higher voltages. Here $V_{oc}$ is only 3.2V.
    *   $3.2\text{V} \times 2 = 6.4\text{V}$. This would definitely hit the Zener.
    *   But it might be more efficient at low frequency?

    *   Let's reconsider the SSHI. The current SSHI is $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
    *   There's another version where the $L$ and $S$ are on the *output* side, but that's basically a buck converter.

    *   How about a "Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor" (SSHI) with a *half-bridge* rectifier?
    *   Wait, if we use a half-bridge (one diode from pzp to out, one capacitor from pzn to 0), the pzn node will drift.
    *   Actually, a common SSHI topology is:
        *   Piezo $C_p$
        *   Inverter $L, S$ in parallel with $C_p$.
        *   Rectifier: D1 (pzp to out), D2 (pzn to out).
        *   Wait, if you have D1 and D2, you still need a path to ground from the piezo.
        *   The current `SSHI_FullBridge_Zener` is:
            *   D1: pzp -> out
            *   D2: pzn -> out
            *   D3: 0 -> pzp
            *   D4: 0 -> pzn
            *   L1, S1: pzp -> pzn
            *   C1: out -> 0
            *   DZ1: 0 -> out
    *   This is a very strong topology. The only failures are marginal ripple and settled.

    *   Can we reduce the ripple by adding a capacitor in parallel to the input (pzp, pzn)?
        *   No, that just increases $C_p$, which the optimizer should have accounted for (it can change $L$ and $S$ values).
    *   Wait, the ripple in S3 is $61\text{mV}$ and the limit is $50\text{mV}$.
    *   S3 has a very light load (RL = 2200 kOhm).
    *   With a light load, $C_{out}$ charges up more.
    *   If $C_{out}$ is larger, the ripple $v_{pp} \approx \Delta Q / C_{out}$ should decrease.
    *   The optimizer has access to $C_{out}$ (C1). Why didn't it increase it?
    *   Maybe $C_{out}$ is limited by $t_{up}$ (startup time)?
    *   In S3, $t_{up} = 0.038\text{s}$. The limit is $0.4\text{s}$. There is plenty of room to increase $C_{out}$.
    *   But the optimizer already tried 48 evaluations. Maybe it reached a local minimum or $C_{out}$ is limited by the $4.7\text{e-05}$ F limit?
    *   Looking at C1 in the best design: $9.33\text{e-07}$ F. This is $0.933 \mu\text{F}$. The limit is $47 \mu\text{F}$.
    *   So $C_{out}$ could be much larger.
    *   Wait, if the optimizer didn't increase $C_{out}$ to reduce ripple, maybe it's because $v_{pp}$ is not primarily driven by $C_{out}$ discharge, but by the *charging* spikes?
    *   In SSHI, the $L-S$ inversion creates a spike. This spike goes through the rectifier into $C_{out}$.
    *   If the spike is large, it increases $v_{max}$ and $v_{pp}$.
    *   To reduce the spike, we can:
        1.  Reduce $L$.
        2.  Reduce $t_{on}$.
        3.  Add a small capacitor to filter the spike.

    *   Let's try adding a small capacitor $C_2$ in parallel with the Zener or the load? (That's just increasing $C_{out}$).
    *   What if we add a capacitor across the rectifier output? (That's also $C_{out}$).
    *   What if we add a capacitor across the piezo *and* the rectifier?
    *   Wait, what if we put a capacitor in series with the rectifier output? No.

    *   Let's try a different topology: **SSHI with a switch-capacitor-inductor combination**? No, too many components.
    *   What about a **Half-Bridge Rectifier** with a **flying capacitor**?
        *   Piezo pzp -> D1 -> out
        *   Piezo pzn -> D2 -> out (wait, this is still a full bridge if there's a ground)
        *   Let's try a simpler rectifier:
            *   D1: pzp -> out
            *   C_fly: pzn -> 0
            *   S1: pzp -> pzn (inversion)
            *   L1: in series with S1.
            *   This is basically a half-bridge SSHI.

    *   Actually, the `SSHI_FullBridge_Zener` is already very good. The failures are $0.061$ vs $0.05$ and $0.022$ vs $0.02$.
    *   What if we replace the Full Bridge with a **Center-Tapped** style? (Not possible, piezo is not center-tapped).
    *   What if we use a **Synchronous Rectifier** for one of the half-cycles?
        *   SYNC1: Inversion (L1, S1)
        *   SYNC2: Rectification?
        *   If we use SYNC2 to close a switch between pzp and out during the positive peak, we reduce the diode drop (0.25V -> 0.002V). This would *increase* the voltage, potentially making the Zener clamp more and *increasing* the ripple.

    *   What if we use a **Low-Pass Filter** (L-C) before the storage capacitor?
        *   Rectifier -> L2 -> C_out.
        *   L2 would block the high-frequency spikes from the SSHI inversion.
        *   Let's try this.
        *   D1-D4: Full Bridge.
        *   L1, S1: Inverter.
        *   L2: between the rectifier output and $C_{out}$.
        *   C1: $C_{out}$.
        *   DZ1: Zener across $C_{out}$.

    *   Wait, if we put $L_2$ in series with $C_{out}$, we create a second-order filter. This should significantly reduce $v_{pp}$.

    *   *Topology Check:*
        *   Piezo: pzp, pzn.
        *   Inverter: L1 (pzp -> n1), S1 (n1 -> pzn).
        *   Full Bridge:
            *   D1 (pzp -> n2)
            *   D2 (pzn -> n2)
            *   D3 (0 -> pzp)
            *   D4 (0 -> pzn)
            *   Wait, this is a weird bridge. Standard:
                *   D1 (pzp -> out)
                *   D2 (pzn -> out)
                *   D3 (0 -> pzp)
                *   D4 (0 -> pzn)
                *   Wait, no. Standard full bridge:
                    *   Two diodes from piezo to `out` (D1, D2)
                    *   Two diodes from `0` to piezo (D3, D4)
                    *   Wait, that's not right.
                    *   Correct: D1 (pzp -> out), D2 (pzn -> out), D3 (0 -> pzp), D4 (0 -> pzn). No, that's not it.
                    *   Correct Full Bridge:
                        *   D1: pzp -> out
                        *   D2: pzn -> out
                        *   D3: 0 -> pzp
                        *   D4: 0 -> pzn
                        *   Wait, let's trace:
                            *   If pzp is +, pzn is -:
                                *   Current: 0 -> D3 -> pzp -> (rectifier) -> out -> 0.
                                *   No, the bridge is:
                                    *   D1: pzp -> out
                                    *   D2: pzn -> out
                                    *   D3: 0 -> pzp
                                    *   D4: 0 -> pzn
                                    *   Wait, this is the same as the reference design. Let's check the reference:
                                        *   "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]"
                                        *   Let's trace this:
                                            *   If pzp=+, pzn=-: Current flows 0 -> D4 -> pzn... no.
                                            *   If pzp=+, pzn=-: D3 is off, D4 is on (0 -> pzn). D1 is on (pzp -> out), D2 is off.
                                            *   Path: 0 -> D4 -> pzn -> piezo -> pzp -> D1 -> out. (Correct).
                                            *   If pzp=-, pzn=+: D4 is off, D3 is on (0 -> pzp). D1 is off, D2 is on (pzn -> out).
                                            *   Path: 0 -> D3 -> pzp -> piezo -> pzn -> D2 -> out. (Correct).

    *   *Adding the LC Filter:*
        *   The rectifier output is `out`.
        *   We need to change the rectifier output node to `n_rect`.
        *   Then add $L_2$ from `n_rect` to `out`.
        *   $C_{out}$ and $R_L$ and $DZ_1$ are at node `out`.

    *   *Components:*
        *   D1: pzp -> n_rect
        *   D2: pzn -> n_rect
        *   D3: 0 -> pzp
        *   D4: 0 -> pzn
        *   L1: pzp -> n1
        *   S1: n1 -> pzn
        *   G1: SYNC
        *   L2: n_rect -> out
        *   C1: out -> 0
        *   DZ1: 0 -> out
        *   (Total components: 10. Limit: 16).
